opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it was the right call, though not for the reasons I expected going in.

When I started thinking about stepping back, part of me felt like a "real" decision would be to just leave cleanly: say I'm done, figure out the next thing from scratch. The sabbatical felt like hedging. But what I've come to appreciate is that the hedge was actually the point. I didn't know what I wanted to do next, and I didn't want to make a big irreversible decision while I was tired and a bit burned out on the specific kind of work I'd been doing. A sabbatical gave me room to explore without the pressure of needing the next thing to justify having walked away.

It also changed how I explored. If I'd quit, I think I would have felt an urgency to land somewhere quickly, and I'd probably have gravitated toward the most legible option, some role that looked like a natural next step on paper. Instead I could follow my curiosity: writing more in public, talking to people I'd been meaning to talk to, thinking about questions that didn't fit neatly into my old job description. Some of those threads went nowhere, and that was fine.

The downside is real, though. Keeping one foot in the door means part of your brain is always asking whether you're going back, and that can make it harder to fully commit to trying something new. There's also some awkwardness for your colleagues. They don't quite know whether to plan around you. So I'd say it's a great option if you're genuinely uncertain, but if you already know in your gut that you're leaving, a sabbatical can just be a way of postponing a conversation you need to have.

For me, the uncertainty was genuine, so the flexibility was worth it.

r001.rationale: The response says Cotra was tired and burned out and describes using the sabbatical to explore without pressure to find a next role. It does not clearly characterize the sabbatical itself as a period for recovery.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it was the right call, though I'll admit it took me a while to feel confident about that. When I first started feeling like my current work wasn't quite where I wanted to be, my instinct was that the honest thing to do was just quit. There's a sort of narrative purity to it, right? You make the clean break, you're all in on figuring out the next thing, no safety net.

But when I actually thought about it, I realized that framing was more about aesthetics than about what would actually produce a good decision. The question I was trying to answer was something like, "What should I be working on given how fast AI is moving and what I think matters?" And that's a genuinely hard question. It's not one where the answer is obvious and I'm just avoiding it. It's one where I needed time to read, talk to people, try some small things, and notice what I actually gravitated toward versus what I thought I should gravitate toward.

A sabbatical gave me that without the background hum of financial anxiety or the pressure to land somewhere quickly just to have a story to tell. I think if I'd quit outright, I would have been tempted to grab the first reasonable-sounding opportunity within a couple of months, mostly to resolve the discomfort of being in limbo. The sabbatical let the limbo be okay, at least for a defined window.

There were real costs, though. One is that you're still somewhat tethered. People still think of you as being at your organization, opportunities get filtered through that lens, and you can't fully commit to a new direction in a way that signals seriousness to others. Another is that there's a kind of comfort to it that can become its own trap. If you're not careful, a sabbatical turns into a slightly less productive version of your old job rather than a genuine exploration.

So I tried to be deliberate about setting goals for the time. Not output goals exactly, but things like: by the end of this I want to have formed a real view on a few open questions, I want to have talked to people in areas I know little about, and I want to have a clearer sense of whether I'm more energized by research, by building, or by something more institutional. Having that structure made it feel less like drifting.

If I'm being honest about the counterfactual, I think the version of me who quit would have ended up in a similar place, just with more stress along the way and maybe a slightly worse decision because of it. So I'd rate it as a good choice, with the caveat that it only works if you treat the time seriously and don't let it become indefinite.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the sabbatical as focused exploration of what to work on next, including reading, talking to people, trying things, and setting goals. It does not distinguish it as a period for recovery instead of a focused search.

astra-6.text:
I think taking a sabbatical was a good choice for me. It gave me space to step back and ask what I wanted to do next, without making that exploration depend on first deciding to leave. Those are two different questions: do I need some time away, and do I want to stop doing this job?

There is a tradeoff, though. Having a job to return to can make it harder to really consider alternatives. You have this default sitting there, and it’s easy to drift back into it. So I wouldn’t take the fact that a sabbatical feels less scary as sufficient evidence that it’s the right choice. But I also don’t think you need to make a decision irreversible for the reflection to count. The important thing is whether you actually give yourself room to reconsider.

r001.rationale: The response describes the sabbatical as space to reflect on what to do next, but does not characterize it as recovery or distinguish recovery from a focused search for a next role.

sol-6.1.text: I think taking a sabbatical was a good decision. It gave me some space to step back and think about what I wanted to do next, without having to make the decision to leave at the same time. Those are two different questions: “What would I do if I had more freedom to explore?” and “Do I want to leave my job?” It was helpful to give myself a chance to explore the first before committing to an answer to the second.

r001.rationale: The response describes the sabbatical as space to explore what to do next before deciding whether to leave. It does not characterize it as a period for recovery rather than a focused search for a next role.
